customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 17: Economic Appraisal and Evaluation of Projects
customPastQuestions.questionText: What are the two types of linkage effects of a project?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Backward linkages are additional activities and demand created among suppliers of inputs needed by a new project, such as transport, building materials, agricultural products or service providers supplying the venture. Forward linkages arise when the project's output provides an input or creates opportunities for other activities that use it. For example, a newly established institution may stimulate nearby accommodation, restaurants and other services, while a processing enterprise can create downstream users of its output. Linkages show how a project can affect other sectors beyond its own direct costs and revenue.
keyRubricPoints: Backward linkages: stimulated demand for input suppliers (raw materials, transport, construction)
Forward linkages: output creates downstream utilization opportunities for other enterprises
Concrete example: polytechnic/institution stimulating private hostels, dining, hair salons

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 1: Sources of Information for Feasibility Studies
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Pre-feasibility vs Detailed Study & Information Sources
customPastQuestions.questionText: Differentiate between a pre-feasibility study and a comprehensive feasibility study, and identify three primary and three secondary sources of data used in feasibility investigations in Nigeria.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
A pre-feasibility study is an initial, exploratory evaluation designed to quickly screen an entrepreneurial idea to determine whether it warrants the substantial time and expenditure of a complete investigation. In contrast, a comprehensive feasibility study is a rigorous, detailed, and exhaustive appraisal of the venture's technical, financial, commercial, and operational viability before committing capital.

Primary data sources in Nigeria include: (1) Direct surveys of potential consumers using questionnaires; (2) In-depth interviews with distributors, wholesalers, and retailers; and (3) Observational traffic counts and competitive mystery shopping.

Secondary data sources include: (1) National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) demographic and trade publications; (2) Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) statistical bulletins and interest rate bulletins; and (3) Publications of statutory promotional agencies such as SMEDAN, NDE, and Chambers of Commerce (LCCI/NACCIMA).
customPastQuestions.modelAnswer: Pre-feasibility serves as preliminary screening; full feasibility provides exhaustive operational and financial verification. Primary sources include surveys, interviews, and direct observations. Secondary sources include NBS, CBN, SMEDAN, and trade associations.
keyRubricPoints: Accurate contrast between preliminary screening (pre-feasibility) and exhaustive viability assessment (full study)
Three authentic primary sources: consumer questionnaires, distributor interviews, direct field observation
Three authentic Nigerian secondary sources: NBS, CBN, SMEDAN/Chambers of Commerce
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 3; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 1 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 2: Generating Data for Feasibility Studies
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Primary Data Gathering and Non-Response Bias
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the structured questionnaire and personal interview methods for gathering market data during feasibility research. What practical measures should an investigator take to minimize non-response bias?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Structured questionnaires use predetermined, sequenced questions (closed-ended and open-ended) to collect standardized quantitative data from a broad sample of respondents efficiently. Personal interviews involve face-to-face dialogue that allows deep probing, immediate clarification of complex queries, and qualitative insight into buyer motivation.

To minimize non-response bias: (1) Keep the questionnaire concise and focused on essential variables; (2) Pre-test the research instrument for ambiguity; (3) Offer non-coercive incentives or professional courtesy explanations; (4) Follow up with non-respondents across multiple communication channels; and (5) Train field enumerators to establish polite rapport and guarantee confidentiality.
keyRubricPoints: Structured questionnaire characteristics: standardization, wide reach, closed vs open questions
Personal interview characteristics: probing, flexibility, high response rate, higher cost
Non-response reduction measures: concise wording, pilot pre-testing, respectful follow-up, assured confidentiality
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 6; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 2 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 3: Business Description
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Business Description Elements and Legal Structure
customPastQuestions.questionText: Detail the critical elements required in the business description section of a feasibility report, highlighting why defining the enterprise's legal form of ownership (Sole Proprietorship, Partnership, Limited Liability Company) is fundamental to feasibility.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
The business description must encompass: (1) Enterprise name, mission, vision, and core values; (2) Nature of business, sector, and industry classification; (3) Distinctive value proposition and product/service portfolio; (4) Growth history or inception background; (5) Ownership and legal form of registration with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC); and (6) Current status and competitive advantage.

Specifying the legal structure is critical because it dictates: (a) Liability exposure of the founders (unlimited personal liability in sole proprietorship/general partnership vs limited liability in LLC); (b) Ability to attract outside debt and equity capital; (c) Tax obligations and statutory compliance requirements under the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA); and (d) Business continuity and perpetual succession upon the death or exit of a founder.
keyRubricPoints: Six essential elements: name/mission, industry classification, product line, inception, legal form, competitive advantage
Liability implications: personal asset vulnerability vs limited corporate shield
Capital access and investor eligibility under CAMA regulations
Perpetual succession and corporate governance continuity
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 9; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 3 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 4: Location or Siting of Business
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Plant Location vs Retail Siting Criteria
customPastQuestions.questionText: Distinguish between plant location factors for a manufacturing enterprise and site location factors for a consumer retail business according to ENT 302 principles.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Manufacturing plant location prioritizes cost minimization, logistics efficiency, and regulatory compliance: (1) Proximity to heavy raw materials (especially where materials are bulky or weight-losing); (2) Availability of reliable industrial power, water, and waste disposal; (3) Access to freight transport arteries (rail, highways, ports); (4) Cost and supply of technical and semi-skilled labor; and (5) Local zoning and environmental protection laws.

In contrast, consumer retail siting is revenue and convenience-driven: (1) Pedestrian foot traffic density and vehicular visibility; (2) Proximity and accessibility to target demographic clusters; (3) Parking convenience and ingress/egress safety; (4) Neighboring tenant synergy and compatible commercial draws; and (5) Lease terms and rent per square meter.
keyRubricPoints: Manufacturing focus: input cost minimization, bulk raw material proximity, industrial infrastructure, freight
Retail focus: customer foot-traffic, visibility, accessibility, demographic purchasing power, parking
Reference to Weberian location principles and NOUN ENT 302 Unit 4 guidelines
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 13; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 4 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 5: Management and Production Unit
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain how management organizational structuring and production planning interact in a new enterprise. Outline the key considerations for determining production capacity and raw material inventory control.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Management structuring creates the division of labor, reporting hierarchy, and supervisory controls necessary to execute the production schedule seamlessly. Without clear delegation, production bottlenecks, wastage, and safety violations escalate.

Key considerations for production capacity: (1) Projected market demand and seasonal peak fluctuations; (2) Rated machine capacity versus realistic effective operating hours; and (3) Availability and downtime for maintenance.

Key considerations for raw materials inventory control: (1) Lead times required by domestic and foreign suppliers; (2) Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) balancing ordering costs against carrying costs; (3) Safety stock margins to prevent stock-outs during logistics disruptions; and (4) Perishability and warehouse storage conditions.
keyRubricPoints: Interaction between organogram/delegation and factory floor execution
Determining capacity: market demand, machine throughput, maintenance downtime
Inventory control variables: supplier lead time, holding vs ordering costs, safety stock buffer
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 16; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 5 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 6: Technical Analysis
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Technical Feasibility and Machinery Selection Criteria
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the scope of technical analysis in a feasibility report. What criteria should guide the entrepreneur in selecting plant equipment, machinery, and production technology?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Technical analysis assesses the physical, engineering, and manufacturing feasibility of the project. It examines whether the product can be produced at acceptable quality standards, within cost budgets, and using proven technology.

Criteria for selecting machinery and technology: (1) Technical suitability and capacity alignment with market demand; (2) Ease of operation and availability of local technical personnel to maintain it; (3) Availability and cost of spare parts locally; (4) Energy efficiency and compatibility with local power supply; (5) Obsolescence risk and flexibility to adapt to future product changes; and (6) Capital acquisition cost versus warranty and supplier after-sales support.
keyRubricPoints: Scope of technical analysis: physical feasibility, engineering specifications, site layout
Selection criteria: throughput capacity, local maintenance expertise, spare parts availability
Energy requirements, technology obsolescence risk, and vendor support
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 19; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 6 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 7: Defining Management Team for Operation Unit
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Management Team Credentials and Investor Scrutiny
customPastQuestions.questionText: Why do financial institutions and investors scrutinize the background, technical qualifications, and track record of the management team when evaluating a feasibility proposal?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Venture capitalists and commercial lenders recognize that a brilliant business idea with mediocre management frequently fails, whereas an experienced, cohesive management team can navigate market uncertainties and execute successfully. Evaluators scrutinize: (1) Relevant industry experience and technical expertise; (2) Complementary skill sets spanning finance, marketing, operations, and leadership; (3) Past managerial track record and integrity; (4) Commitment to the venture (including personal financial equity stake); and (5) Succession planning and key-man insurance to mitigate reliance on a single individual.
keyRubricPoints: Investor adage: backing the jockey (management) over the horse (idea)
Scrutiny dimensions: industry track record, complementary functional skills, personal equity commitment
Key-man risk and governance succession
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 22; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 7 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 8: Market Analysis and Marketing Plan
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Market Segmentation and Total Addressable Market Sizing
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the four bases of market segmentation (geographic, demographic, psychographic, and behavioral) and explain how an entrepreneur calculates Total Addressable Market (TAM) and market share in feasibility planning.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
The four bases of segmentation are: (1) Geographic: location, urban/rural density, climate, state/region; (2) Demographic: age, gender, household income, education, occupation; (3) Psychographic: lifestyle, social class, values, personal aspirations; and (4) Behavioral: usage frequency, brand loyalty, purchase readiness, price sensitivity.

Calculating TAM and Market Share: TAM is the total annual market demand or revenue potential if 100% of the target population purchased the product (Total Target Customers × Average Annual Consumption × Unit Price). Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM) is the portion reachable by the enterprise's channels. Projected Market Share is the percentage of SAM the new firm realistically captures within 1 to 3 years based on production capacity, competitor strength, and marketing expenditure.
keyRubricPoints: Detailed breakdown of all four segmentation criteria with practical examples
Formulaic and conceptual derivation of Total Addressable Market (TAM)
Realistic market share estimation factoring production constraints and competitors
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 25; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 8 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 9: Defining Marketing Strategies
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Price Penetration vs Price Skimming Strategies
customPastQuestions.questionText: Evaluate price penetration versus price skimming strategies for a newly introduced product. In what market conditions is each pricing strategy recommended?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Price Penetration sets an initially low price to attract high sales volume rapidly, deter competitors, and capture dominant market share. It is recommended when: (1) Market demand is price elastic (highly sensitive to price); (2) Economies of scale can be achieved quickly at high production volumes; and (3) Intense competition threatens fast follower entry.

Price Skimming sets an initially premium price to recover heavy R&D and launch costs from less price-sensitive early adopters before lowering prices systematically. It is recommended when: (1) The product has high perceived prestige, distinctive uniqueness, or patent protection; (2) Demand is inelastic; (3) Production capacity is initially limited; and (4) Competitors cannot enter the market immediately.
keyRubricPoints: Price Penetration: low entry price, mass volume, high price elasticity, scale economies
Price Skimming: premium entry price, margin recovery, unique value/patents, low price elasticity
Market conditions justifying each strategy
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 28; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 9 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 10: Business Plan Implementation
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Gantt Charts and Implementation Risk Mitigation
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the role of the Gantt chart and milestone scheduling in business plan implementation. What operational risks cause delays in project execution?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
A Gantt chart visually maps project activities, their start dates, durations, task dependencies, and scheduled completion milestones along a calendar timeline. It enables management to identify the critical path, allocate physical and financial resources synchronously, and monitor variance between planned and actual progress.

Operational risks causing execution delays include: (1) Delays in statutory approvals, environmental permits, and CAC registration; (2) Machinery procurement, shipping customs bottlenecks, and port clearing delays; (3) Construction cost overruns and building contractor non-performance; (4) Key personnel recruitment and training shortfalls; and (5) Working capital cash deficits resulting from delayed loan disbursements.
keyRubricPoints: Gantt chart functionality: visual timeline, activity dependencies, critical path, variance monitoring
Key milestone markers: CAC incorporation, site acquisition, machine commissioning, commercial launch
Operational delay risks: regulatory approvals, customs/shipping, contractor defaults, cash flow timing
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 31; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 10 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 11: Financial Analysis
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Break-Even Point (BEP) and Margin of Safety Numerical Analysis
customPastQuestions.questionText: Define Break-Even Point (BEP). Given that a firm has fixed costs of N1,200,000, variable cost per unit of N400, and selling price per unit of N700, calculate: (i) Break-even volume in units, (ii) Break-even revenue in Naira, and (iii) Margin of safety if anticipated sales are 6,000 units.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Break-Even Point (BEP) is the level of operations where total revenue exactly equals total costs, yielding neither profit nor loss.

Formulae & Calculations:
Contribution margin per unit (CM) = Selling Price (P) - Variable Cost per unit (VC) = N700 - N400 = N300.

(i) BEP (units) = Fixed Costs / CM = N1,200,000 / N300 = 4,000 units.

(ii) BEP (revenue) = BEP (units) × Selling Price = 4,000 × N700 = N2,800,000.
Alternatively: FC / (CM / P) = N1,200,000 / (300 / 700) = N2,800,000.

(iii) Margin of Safety:
In units = Budgeted Sales - BEP Sales = 6,000 - 4,000 = 2,000 units.
In value = 2,000 × N700 = N1,400,000.
In percentage = (Budgeted Sales - BEP Sales) / Budgeted Sales = (6,000 - 4,000) / 6,000 × 100% = 33.33%.

workedSolutionSteps.description: Calculate BEP Volume in Units (FC / CM)

keyRubricPoints: Formal definition of Break-Even Point as zero-profit threshold
Step 1: Unit contribution margin of N300
Step 2: Correct BEP volume of 4,000 units
Step 3: Correct BEP sales revenue of N2,800,000
Step 4: Margin of safety: 2,000 units, N1,400,000, or 33.33%
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 34; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 11 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 12: Financing Plan
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Debt vs Equity Financing and the 5 Cs of Credit
customPastQuestions.questionText: Compare debt financing and equity financing in capital structuring for a new venture. Explain the '5 Cs of Credit' used by commercial bankers to assess loan applications.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Debt financing involves borrowed capital that must be repaid with interest according to a contractual amortization schedule, regardless of profitability, but does not dilute voting ownership. Equity financing involves issuing ownership shares in exchange for permanent capital without mandatory interest obligations, but dilutes control and entitles investors to residual profits.

The 5 Cs of Credit evaluated by commercial banks are: (1) Character: the borrower's reputation, integrity, and credit history; (2) Capacity: cash flow generation ability to comfortably service debt repayments; (3) Capital: the founder's personal equity invested in the venture (skin in the game); (4) Collateral: pledgeable assets securing the loan in case of default; and (5) Conditions: macroeconomic environment, interest rate trends, and industry viability.
keyRubricPoints: Debt vs Equity contrast: interest obligation vs ownership dilution, bankruptcy risk vs control
Character: borrower integrity and track record
Capacity: cash flow debt-service coverage
Capital: owner equity commitment
Collateral: pledged security assets
Conditions: economic and industry climate
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 37; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 12 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 13: Preparing Business Proposals
customPastQuestions.questionText: What is an Executive Summary, and why is it often considered the single most critical section of a business proposal presented to prospective investors?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
The Executive Summary is a concise, high-level synthesis of the entire business proposal, typically spanning 1 to 2 pages, capturing the business model, target market, competitive edge, management team qualifications, capital funding requirement, and financial return forecasts.

It is the most critical section because: (1) It is the first (and sometimes only) section busy loan officers and angel investors read; (2) It serves as a gateway filter determining whether the reader commits time to review the complete proposal; (3) It articulates the venture's core investment thesis and value proposition succinctly; and (4) It showcases managerial clarity and commercial professionalism.
keyRubricPoints: Definition of Executive Summary as 1-2 page synthesis of business model and returns
Gateway filter role: decisive factor in whether investors read further
Key components included: concept, problem solved, team, financing sought, expected ROI
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 40; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 13 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 14: Cash Flow Analysis
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Net Profit vs Net Cash Flow and Insolvency Dynamics
customPastQuestions.questionText: Distinguish between accounting net profit and net cash flow. Why is a profitable enterprise still vulnerable to insolvency if cash flow forecasting is poorly managed?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Accounting net profit is computed on an accrual basis (Revenue earned minus Expenses incurred), recording revenue at the point of sale whether cash has been received or not, and recognizing non-cash deductions such as depreciation. Net cash flow measures actual liquid money received minus liquid money disbursed during the accounting period.

A business can be highly profitable on paper yet collapse into technical insolvency if: (1) Substantial revenues are locked up in uncollected accounts receivable (credit sales); (2) High cash outlays are required upfront for inventory and raw materials before sales occur; (3) Heavy debt principal repayments must be serviced (which do not appear on the income statement as expenses); and (4) Large capital expenditure commitments exhaust cash reserves.
keyRubricPoints: Accrual accounting basis (profit) versus liquidity timing (cash flow)
Non-cash items (depreciation) and balance sheet movements (principal repayment)
Four causes of profitable failure: credit customer delays, inventory buildup, debt principal drain, capital expenditures
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 42; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 14 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 15: Traditional Investment Appraisal Methods
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Payback Period Calculation and Traditional Method Limitations
customPastQuestions.questionText: An investment requires an initial cash outlay of N5,000,000 and generates annual net cash inflows of N1,500,000, N2,000,000, N1,800,000, and N1,200,000 over four years. Calculate the Payback Period, and discuss two major limitations of the traditional payback method.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Cumulative cash flow schedule:
Year 0: (N5,000,000)
Year 1 inflow: N1,500,000 -> Cumulative recovered: N1,500,000 (Remaining: N3,500,000)
Year 2 inflow: N2,000,000 -> Cumulative recovered: N3,500,000 (Remaining: N1,500,000)
Year 3 inflow: N1,800,000 -> Inflow exceeds required N1,500,000.
Fraction of Year 3 needed = N1,500,000 / N1,800,000 = 0.833 years.
Payback Period = 2 years + 0.833 years = 2.83 years (approximately 2 years and 10 months).

Two major limitations:
(1) Ignores the Time Value of Money: It treats N1 received in Year 4 equally to N1 received in Year 1 without discounting for inflation or cost of capital.
(2) Ignores cash flows occurring after the payback threshold: A project that yields massive profits in Year 4 and 5 could be rejected in favor of a project that breaks even slightly earlier but yields nothing thereafter.

workedSolutionSteps.description: Compute Cumulative Cash Flows for Years 1 & 2

keyRubricPoints: Accurate cumulative cash flow calculation for Years 1 and 2
Correct fractional interpolation of 0.83 years
Final answer: 2.83 years or 2 years 10 months
Limitation 1: Neglects Time Value of Money
Limitation 2: Ignores cash flows beyond the cut-off payback date
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 44; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 15 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 16: Discounted Cash Flow Methods of Appraisal
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Discounted Cash Flow Decision Rules and NPV vs IRR Conflicts
customPastQuestions.questionText: State the decision rules for Net Present Value (NPV), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), and Profitability Index (PI). In the event of conflicting rankings between NPV and IRR for mutually exclusive projects, which criterion should the financial analyst prioritize and why?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Decision Rules:
(1) Net Present Value (NPV): Accept if NPV > 0; Reject if NPV < 0; Indifferent if NPV = 0.
(2) Internal Rate of Return (IRR): Accept if IRR > Cost of Capital (r); Reject if IRR < r.
(3) Profitability Index (PI): Accept if PI > 1.0; Reject if PI < 1.0.

Conflicting Rankings: For mutually exclusive projects with differing cash flow timings or unequal scales of investment, NPV and IRR may give conflicting rankings. The financial analyst must prioritize NPV. NPV measures the absolute net addition to total shareholder wealth in currency value (Naira), whereas IRR is a relative percentage rate that implicitly assumes cash inflows are reinvested at the internal rate of return rather than the enterprise's realistic cost of capital.
keyRubricPoints: Formal acceptance criteria for NPV (>0), IRR (>r), and PI (>1)
Identification of reasons for conflict: scale differences and reinvestment rate assumptions
Superiority of NPV based on shareholder wealth maximization
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 46; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 16 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 17: Economic Appraisal and Evaluation of Projects
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Social Cost-Benefit Analysis and Shadow Pricing
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the rationale for Social Cost-Benefit Analysis (SCBA) in public-private project appraisal. What are shadow prices, and why must market prices of labor and foreign currency be adjusted in developing economies like Nigeria?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Social Cost-Benefit Analysis (SCBA) assesses a project from the perspective of the entire society and national economy rather than the narrow commercial profitability of private shareholders. It evaluates whether the project contributes net social welfare, generates employment, saves foreign exchange, and creates backward/forward economic linkages.

Shadow prices represent the true social opportunity cost of economic resources when prevailing market prices are distorted by taxes, subsidies, import tariffs, price controls, or monopolistic practices.

Adjustments in developing economies like Nigeria:
(1) Shadow Wage Rate for Unskilled Labor: In an economy with widespread underemployment, the market minimum wage exceeds the true opportunity cost of labor (foregone agricultural output). Shadow wages reflect this lower opportunity cost.
(2) Shadow Exchange Rate: Official foreign exchange rates often overvalue local currency due to import rationing, so foreign currency saved or spent must be valued at its true scarcity value (shadow exchange rate) to prevent distorted project selection.
keyRubricPoints: Distinction between private commercial profitability and national social welfare
Definition of shadow price as true economic opportunity cost adjusting for market distortions
Shadow wage rate rationale under structural unemployment
Shadow foreign exchange rate rationale under foreign exchange scarcity
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 48; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 17 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.questionText: Outline the steps involved in constructing a Competitor Profiling Matrix during market feasibility analysis.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Steps to construct a Competitor Profiling Matrix: (1) Identify direct, indirect, and future substitute competitors in the target market; (2) Determine key success factors (KSFs) in the industry (e.g., pricing, product quality, brand reputation, distribution reach, customer service); (3) Assign weighting to each success factor according to market significance; (4) Rate each competitor and the new venture against these factors on a standardized scale (1 to 5); and (5) Calculate composite scores to reveal competitive vulnerabilities and strategic opportunities.

customPastQuestions.questionText: Compare direct marketing channels (manufacturer to consumer) with indirect channels (wholesalers and retailers) in the Nigerian business environment.

customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Development Finance Institutions in Nigeria (BOI & SMEDAN)
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the role of Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) like the Bank of Industry (BOI) in providing concessionary long-term credit to small and medium manufacturing enterprises in Nigeria.

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 16: Discounted Cash Flow Methods of Appraisal
customPastQuestions.questionText: State the Profitability Index (Benefit-Cost Ratio) formula and explain how it resolves capital rationing when an entrepreneur has multiple positive NPV projects but limited capital.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Profitability Index (PI) = Present Value of Future Cash Inflows / Initial Cash Outlay = PV / I0. In capital rationing where capital is constrained, ranking projects by absolute NPV can be suboptimal because large projects absorb all capital while yielding lower return per Naira invested. Ranking by Profitability Index identifies the combination of projects that generates the highest total net present value per unit of constrained capital.

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 1: Concept and Meaning of Leadership
customPastQuestions.questionText: Using not less than ten items, attempt the definition of leadership.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Leadership can be understood through ten connected ideas: (1) influencing others; (2) directing collective effort; (3) communicating a vision; (4) giving people a clear purpose; (5) achieving a shared goal; (6) building trust; (7) motivating willing participation; (8) recognising people's strengths; (9) taking responsibility and leading by example; and (10) helping followers develop their abilities. Effective leadership relies on appropriate use of these powers rather than fear alone.

customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Transactional leadership rests on a clear exchange between leader and followers. Unlike transformational leadership, the central emphasis is normally meeting established objectives rather than altering followers' values and aspirations.

customPastQuestions.questionText: Differentiate between limitations and delimitations in research.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Delimitations are intentional boundaries imposed by the researcher to make the study specific and manageable: choosing a particular study centre, limiting the period to one semester or investigating only 300-level students. customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 9: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Research
customPastQuestions.questionText: Define Experimental Research and discuss its main characteristics; briefly explain the concept and three characteristics of experimental research.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Experimental research is systematic investigation of a possible cause-and-effect relationship by deliberately varying an independent variable and observing an outcome while other relevant conditions are controlled. Its three principal characteristics are control (hold constant or minimise influences outside the treatment), manipulation (introduce different treatment conditions) and observation (measure responses or dependent-variable changes after the treatment). For example, a researcher may compare customer-service performance after two different staff-training arrangements, while controlling relevant conditions. Strong experiments also describe their participants, instruments and method of comparison clearly.

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 12: Population, Sampling and Sample Size Determination
customPastQuestions.questionText: Differentiate between Probability and Non-Probability Sampling techniques.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: In probability sampling, selection follows a chance procedure and each element has a known probability of inclusion. Techniques include simple random, systematic, stratified random and cluster sampling. It usually improves representativeness, supports statistical inference and permits estimation of sampling error, but may require a suitable population list and more resources. In non-probability sampling, the researcher selects respondents without known inclusion chances, using accessibility, judgment, quotas or referrals. It can be cheaper and suitable for exploratory or hard-to-reach groups, but selection bias is harder to assess and findings should not automatically be generalised statistically to the whole population. The essential distinction is random selection with known chances versus non-random selection without known chances. -- 18 of 24 -- 09163490176 PSALMDATA - TELECOM AND COMPUTER CAFE Motto: I CAN DO ALL THINGS Website: http://psalmedu.com Contacts: 09163490176; 09011055579 RC7712800 PLEASE PATRONIZE US FOR MORE EXAM SUMMARIES, TMA SUBMISSION WITH GOOD GRADES ADMISSION PROCESSING. customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: The six components in the NOUN material are (1) Chapter One – Introduction: background, problem, objectives, questions/hypotheses, significance and scope; (2) Chapter Two – Literature Review: relevant theories, concepts, studies and gaps; (3) Chapter Three – Methodology: proposed design, population, sample, instruments, data collection and analysis; (4) Time Schedule: expected timing of major research activities; (5) Proposal Budget: estimated expenses and resources; and (6) Supplementary Pages: relevant references and appendices. For an ordinary degree proposal, the first three chapters form the core; the course specifically says time schedules and budgets are generally associated with grants/contracts, not the normal supervisor or faculty-defence proposal.

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 15: Ethical Considerations in Scientific Research
customPastQuestions.questionText: Describe six ethical issues in research.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: (1) Informed consent: explain the purpose and procedures and obtain voluntary agreement. (2) Freedom to participate: do not coerce respondents or violate free informed choice. (3) Confidentiality: protect sensitive personal and institutional information. (4) Permission for institutional data: seek prior approval before accessing or publishing information supplied for restricted purposes. (5) Protection from harm: avoid unjustified physical, emotional, psychological, political, moral or economic risks. (6) Honesty and objectivity: collect and present information truthfully and distinguish internal monitoring findings from results authorised for public release. Proposal Versus Completed Report Proposal: tells what the researcher will investigate; usually presents the first three chapters and planned methods. Final report: tells what the researcher did, the results obtained, what they mean and the conclusions drawn. Both must use appropriate referencing and follow ethical requirements. Quick Revision: Proposal = planned work/future tense; report = completed work/results. Ethical research protects consent, confidentiality, permission, safety and truthfulness. EXAMINATION STUDY CHECK Across the supplied papers, pay particular attention to research characteristics and purposes; the four scientific assumptions; hypothesis versus theory; questionnaire construction, qualities and pilot testing; definitions of terms; delimitations versus limitations; observational standards; qualitative and case-study procedures; descriptive/survey research; experimental and action research; sampling; mean/median/mode and normal curve; proposal components; and ethical issues. The two copies of the 2024_1 paper were identical and have been counted as one session. The 2023_1 paper carries a different course-title wording ('Research Methods for Business Decisions'), but the course code is FMS 304 and the supplied 2023 NOUN course material is titled 'Research Methodology'. For consistency this summary follows the material's title and structure. SOURCE NOTE: Prepared strictly from the supplied FMS 304 NOUN course material and six distinct examination sessions (seven files). Where a paper requests information absent from the material, that gap is identified rather than filled from outside sources. -- 24 of 24 --
